items.stem: ‘The leaders of big business in the Gilded Age were robber barons who harmed the American economy.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: They used ruthless methods such as rebates, price-cutting and bribery. Monopolies kept prices high and crushed small firms. Workers suffered low wages and dangerous conditions. Against: They built efficient industries that lowered prices, such as kerosene and steel. They created jobs and made the US the leading industrial power. Philanthropists such as Carnegie gave away fortunes. Judgement: their methods were often ruthless, but they were also "industrial statesmen" whose organisation drove growth; the harm fell more on competitors and workers than on the economy as a whole.

items.stem: How far was government policy responsible for the rapid industrial growth of the USA after 1870?
items.answer: For: High tariffs protected industry. Land grants helped build railroads. Laissez-faire allowed business to grow without regulation. Judgement: government policy helped, but growth depended mainly on resources, markets, labour and enterprise.

items.stem: In 1911 a fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York killed 146 workers. Explain why trade unions found it hard to improve workers' conditions before 1914.
items.answer: Employers used lockouts, blacklists and strike-breakers. Courts issued injunctions and federal troops broke strikes such as Pullman. Workers were divided by skill, ethnicity and race. items.stem: Felix is planning an answer to the question: “‘The Populist movement was a failure.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Felix could use to support the view and two to challenge it.

items.stem: Grace is planning an answer to the question: “‘The leaders of big business in the Gilded Age were robber barons who harmed the American economy.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Grace could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: their methods were often ruthless, but they were also "industrial statesmen" whose organisation drove growth; the harm fell more on competitors and workers than on the economy as a whole. Support: They used ruthless methods such as rebates, price-cutting and bribery. Monopolies kept prices high and crushed small firms. Challenge: They built efficient industries that lowered prices, such as kerosene and steel. They created jobs and made the US the leading industrial power.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Study all the sources. Source A: Andrew Carnegie, The Gospel of Wealth, 1889 (summary). Carnegie argued that competition was hard on individuals but best for the race, and that the rich should use their surplus wealth during their lifetimes for the good of the community. Source B: a cartoon in a popular magazine, 1880s (description). The cartoon shows a giant oil tank with tentacles wrapped around the Capitol, a state house and small businesses. “The leaders of big business were "robber barons" who harmed the American economy.” How far do Sources A and B support this view?
items.answer: Source A challenges: it presents big business as beneficial. Evaluation: Carnegie was defending himself and his class. Source B supports: it presents Standard Oil as harmful. Evaluation: it is satire designed to make a point, not a balanced view. Grouping: support B; challenge A. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.

items.stem: Explain why so many immigrants came to the USA between 1870 and 1920.
items.answer: Jobs in expanding industries pulled migrants to the USA. Poverty, rural overpopulation and persecution, such as of Jews in Russia, pushed people out of Europe. Judgement: the pull of industrial jobs was the main reason, made easier by cheap transport.
